newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai gold demand rising on Indian demand.
newsitem.headline: Dubai gold demand rising on Indian demand.

text.p: Gold demand in the Gulf trading hub of Dubai is showing early signs of an upturn ahead of the Indian fourth quarter festival season after months of subdued summer trade, bullion traders based in Dubai said on Sunday.
"Daily trade compared to August is picking up. Before soon it will return back to normal," one souk seller said.
The main Indian festival season will fall in November, meaning that Gulf and Indian subcontinent goldsmiths would begin securing their supplies from early October, Dubai traders said.
Indian wedding and festival demand for gold is the prime motor behind the country's huge appetite for bullion that makes India the world's single largest gold consumer market.
Indian bullion demand was subdued in July and August because of monsoon rains while local Gulf interest was checked by the sweltering summer months which led many to leave for vacation.
Cooler Gulf temperatures has brought most Gulf nationals and expatriate workers back to Dubai after summer holoidays, increasing business turnover at local markets, traders said.
Higher oil prices as a result of the latest U.S-Iraq tension were also said by traders to provide a bullish backdrop for fourth quarter demand as liquidity in Gulf economies increases.
World oil prices hit their highest level since the 1990-1991 Gulf War last week as the U.S. military build up in the Gulf increased ahead of an expected strike against Iraq.
"The market is definitely set to improve...the next six months should see better market conditions," a trader said.

Dubai's benchmark Ten Tola bar (TT) -- 3.746 ounces of 24 carat gold -- was quoted at 5,285 UAE dirhams ($1,440.05), down 36 dirhams on the week, tracking prices which have fallen to their lowest level since July on fears of an IMF gold sale.

Spot bullion was last quoted at $382.25-75 an ounce on Saturday following market unease that the IMF could agree this week to sell around five million of the Fund's 104 million ounces of gold to help the world's poorest countries.
Ten gram pieces in Dubai were quoted around 451 dirhams.
Re-export trade opportunities to India were being capped by the weaker rupee value that partly offset the decline in outright dollar-denominated gold prices, local traders said.
The rupee was last quoted at 35.77/78 against the U.S. dollar, its weakest level since February. ($1-3.67 dirhams).
